case_info.scenario: A previously healthy 67-year-old man was referred to the otolaryngology department due to a progressively worsening sore throat over several weeks that was associated with an unintentional 5-kg weight loss and night sweats. The patient did not report recent travel, nor autoimmune conditions, and reported only heterosexual intercourse. A physical examination revealed a mobile, nontender left-sided jugular lymph node. Dentition and oropharyngeal examinations were unremarkable. Results of flexible laryngoscopy were normal. Routine blood work findings showed an elevated C-reactive protein level and a polyclonal elevation of gamma globulins. Complete blood cell count, kidney markers, and liver enzymes were normal. Computed tomographic (CT) angiography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was unremarkable. Due to substantial worsening of the patient’s symptoms during the next weeks, positron emission tomography/CT was performed, with results showing intense bilateral tonsillar hypermetabolism and abnormal lymph node hypermetabolism above and below the diaphragm (Figure 1A). The patient underwent unilateral tonsillectomy followed by a course of antibiotics and prednisone. On pathologic examination, the tonsils showed lymphoid follicular hyperplasia associated with a polymorphic inflammatory infiltrate without abnormal lymphoid cells and plasmocytes (Figure 1B). Further exploration of the patient’s history revealed that 1 year before the otolaryngology evaluation, he developed a cutaneous eruption on the trunk.

options.B: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the tonsil

B, Low-powered (original magnification ×40) and high-powered (inset; original magnification ×400) hematoxylin-eosin stain after tonsillectomy showing lymphoid follicular hyperplasia with a polymorphic inflammatory infiltrate.
case_info.explanation: Almost 1 year after initial presentation, a pathology review of the tonsils found strong positive immunostaining of antitreponemal antibody (Figure 2) associated with a rapid plasma reagin (RPR) blood titer of 1:4. Treponemal antibody test (chemiluminescent immunoassay) confirmed the syphilis diagnosis. The patient received intramuscular injections of 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin G once a week for 3 weeks, with rapid and complete regression of his symptoms. Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection with increased incidence in high-income countries over the past several decades,1with the majority of cases found in men who have sex with men. Acquired syphilis is divided into early syphilis (primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis [ie, acquired within 1 year]) and late syphilis (late latent and tertiary syphilis [ie, acquired after 1 or more years or unknown duration]). Primary syphilis typically begins with a painless ulcer at the site of infection, which can be overlooked when located in the oropharynx, vagina, or rectum. Consequently, many individuals consult clinicians during the secondary stage, which can have various presentations, the most common being a generalized, nonitchy, erythematous maculopapular rash affecting the palms of the hands and soles of the feet. Herein, retrospective analysis of the cutaneous eruption 1 year before otolaryngologist referral could suggest secondary syphilis, although RPR and treponemal antibody tests were not performed at that time. Secondary syphilis comprises other symptoms, such as lymphadenopathy, fever, and asthenia. After untreated infection, tertiary syphilis can develop, leading to severe neurological and cardiac complications. Syphilis of the tonsils rarely presents as a symptom of secondary syphilis. At this stage, the condition presents as bilateral tonsillitis rather than unilateral tonsillitis, as in primary syphilis.2Although tonsils usually exhibit redness, swelling, and a gray exudate, often with a diffuse pharyngitis, initial clinical examination can be normal, and tonsillitis is only revealed by positron emission tomography/CT.3,4It is predominantly associated with cervical or generalized lymphadenopathy. Diagnosis is often delayed and performed using a histopathological analysis (tonsil or lymph node) and fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption. Confirmation with treponemal antibody test is required because of high false positivity rate of RPR, up to 15%, and treponemal immunohistochemical stain is not specific ofTreponema pallidumand can cross-react with commensal spirochetes of the gastrointestinal tract. Because syphilis cases are increased among men who have sex with men, thorough sexual history might also orientate laboratory workup.5 Regarding differential diagnoses, Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease is a benign evolving necrotizing histiocytic lymphadenitis mainly described in Asia. It occurs in young women in the context of an infectious or autoimmune condition. It typically presents with painful persistent cervical lymphadenopathy associated with fever and leukopenia.6Excisional biopsy of a lymph node is essential for the diagnosis, showing paracortical areas of fibrinoid necrosis, abundant karyorrhexis, and mononuclear cell infiltration.7 Tonsils are a frequent site of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the Waldeyer ring.8It is a rare subtype of extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma occurring predominantly in older men and presenting as odynophagia with cervical lymphadenopathy. Histopathological analysis shows proliferation of large-sized tumor cells with pleomorphic nuclei and immunohistochemistry stains positive for B-cell antigens with a high Ki67 proliferation index.9 Primary tonsillar tuberculosis represents a rare presentation of extrapulmonary tuberculosis. Patients present with recurrent or chronic tonsillitis associated with cervical lymphadenopathy and coexisting pulmonary disease. Diagnosis is based on histopathological examination of the tonsil showing epithelioid granulomas and areas of caseous necrosis. Coloration of Ziehl-Neelsen is frequently positive in this location, showing acid-fast bacilli.10 Syphilis has diverse presentations and is referred to as the “great masquerader.” Given this and the increasing incidence of syphilis, a nontreponemal blood test could be included in the diagnosis approach when facing persistent sore throat and lymphadenopathy.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Almost 1 year after initial presentation, a pathology review of the tonsils found strong positive immunostaining of antitreponemal antibody (Figure 2) associated with a rapid plasma reagin (RPR) blood titer of 1:4. Treponemal antibody test (chemiluminescent immunoassay) confirmed the syphilis diagnosis. The patient received intramuscular injections of 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin G once a week for 3 weeks, with rapid and complete regression of his symptoms. Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection with increased incidence in high-income countries over the past several decades,1with the majority of cases found in men who have sex with men. Acquired syphilis is divided into early syphilis (primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis [ie, acquired within 1 year]) and late syphilis (late latent and tertiary syphilis [ie, acquired after 1 or more years or unknown duration]). Primary syphilis typically begins with a painless ulcer at the site of infection, which can be overlooked when located in the oropharynx, vagina, or rectum. Consequently, many individuals consult clinicians during the secondary stage, which can have various presentations, the most common being a generalized, nonitchy, erythematous maculopapular rash affecting the palms of the hands and soles of the feet. Herein, retrospective analysis of the cutaneous eruption 1 year before otolaryngologist referral could suggest secondary syphilis, although RPR and treponemal antibody tests were not performed at that time. Secondary syphilis comprises other symptoms, such as lymphadenopathy, fever, and asthenia. After untreated infection, tertiary syphilis can develop, leading to severe neurological and cardiac complications. Syphilis of the tonsils rarely presents as a symptom of secondary syphilis. At this stage, the condition presents as bilateral tonsillitis rather than unilateral tonsillitis, as in primary syphilis.2Although tonsils usually exhibit redness, swelling, and a gray exudate, often with a diffuse pharyngitis, initial clinical examination can be normal, and tonsillitis is only revealed by positron emission tomography/CT.3,4It is predominantly associated with cervical or generalized lymphadenopathy. Diagnosis is often delayed and performed using a histopathological analysis (tonsil or lymph node) and fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption. Confirmation with treponemal antibody test is required because of high false positivity rate of RPR, up to 15%, and treponemal immunohistochemical stain is not specific ofTreponema pallidumand can cross-react with commensal spirochetes of the gastrointestinal tract. Because syphilis cases are increased among men who have sex with men, thorough sexual history might also orientate laboratory workup.5 Regarding differential diagnoses, Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease is a benign evolving necrotizing histiocytic lymphadenitis mainly described in Asia. It occurs in young women in the context of an infectious or autoimmune condition. It typically presents with painful persistent cervical lymphadenopathy associated with fever and leukopenia.6Excisional biopsy of a lymph node is essential for the diagnosis, showing paracortical areas of fibrinoid necrosis, abundant karyorrhexis, and mononuclear cell infiltration.7 Tonsils are a frequent site of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the Waldeyer ring.8It is a rare subtype of extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma occurring predominantly in older men and presenting as odynophagia with cervical lymphadenopathy. Histopathological analysis shows proliferation of large-sized tumor cells with pleomorphic nuclei and immunohistochemistry stains positive for B-cell antigens with a high Ki67 proliferation index.9 Primary tonsillar tuberculosis represents a rare presentation of extrapulmonary tuberculosis. Patients present with recurrent or chronic tonsillitis associated with cervical lymphadenopathy and coexisting pulmonary disease. Diagnosis is based on histopathological examination of the tonsil showing epithelioid granulomas and areas of caseous necrosis. Coloration of Ziehl-Neelsen is frequently positive in this location, showing acid-fast bacilli.10 Syphilis has diverse presentations and is referred to as the “great masquerader.” Given this and the increasing incidence of syphilis, a nontreponemal blood test could be included in the diagnosis approach when facing persistent sore throat and lymphadenopathy.

case_info.explanation: Almost 1 year after initial presentation, a pathology review of the tonsils found strong positive immunostaining of antitreponemal antibody (Figure 2) associated with a rapid plasma reagin (RPR) blood titer of 1:4. Treponemal antibody test (chemiluminescent immunoassay) confirmed the syphilis diagnosis. The patient received intramuscular injections of 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin G once a week for 3 weeks, with rapid and complete regression of his symptoms. Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection with increased incidence in high-income countries over the past several decades,1with the majority of cases found in men who have sex with men. Acquired syphilis is divided into early syphilis (primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis [ie, acquired within 1 year]) and late syphilis (late latent and tertiary syphilis [ie, acquired after 1 or more years or unknown duration]). Primary syphilis typically begins with a painless ulcer at the site of infection, which can be overlooked when located in the oropharynx, vagina, or rectum. Consequently, many individuals consult clinicians during the secondary stage, which can have various presentations, the most common being a generalized, nonitchy, erythematous maculopapular rash affecting the palms of the hands and soles of the feet. Herein, retrospective analysis of the cutaneous eruption 1 year before otolaryngologist referral could suggest secondary syphilis, although RPR and treponemal antibody tests were not performed at that time. Secondary syphilis comprises other symptoms, such as lymphadenopathy, fever, and asthenia. After untreated infection, tertiary syphilis can develop, leading to severe neurological and cardiac complications. Syphilis of the tonsils rarely presents as a symptom of secondary syphilis. At this stage, the condition presents as bilateral tonsillitis rather than unilateral tonsillitis, as in primary syphilis.2Although tonsils usually exhibit redness, swelling, and a gray exudate, often with a diffuse pharyngitis, initial clinical examination can be normal, and tonsillitis is only revealed by positron emission tomography/CT.3,4It is predominantly associated with cervical or generalized lymphadenopathy. Diagnosis is often delayed and performed using a histopathological analysis (tonsil or lymph node) and fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption. Confirmation with treponemal antibody test is required because of high false positivity rate of RPR, up to 15%, and treponemal immunohistochemical stain is not specific ofTreponema pallidumand can cross-react with commensal spirochetes of the gastrointestinal tract. Because syphilis cases are increased among men who have sex with men, thorough sexual history might also orientate laboratory workup.5 Regarding differential diagnoses, Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease is a benign evolving necrotizing histiocytic lymphadenitis mainly described in Asia. It occurs in young women in the context of an infectious or autoimmune condition. It typically presents with painful persistent cervical lymphadenopathy associated with fever and leukopenia.6Excisional biopsy of a lymph node is essential for the diagnosis, showing paracortical areas of fibrinoid necrosis, abundant karyorrhexis, and mononuclear cell infiltration.7 Tonsils are a frequent site of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the Waldeyer ring.8It is a rare subtype of extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma occurring predominantly in older men and presenting as odynophagia with cervical lymphadenopathy. Histopathological analysis shows proliferation of large-sized tumor cells with pleomorphic nuclei and immunohistochemistry stains positive for B-cell antigens with a high Ki67 proliferation index.9 Primary tonsillar tuberculosis represents a rare presentation of extrapulmonary tuberculosis. Patients present with recurrent or chronic tonsillitis associated with cervical lymphadenopathy and coexisting pulmonary disease. Diagnosis is based on histopathological examination of the tonsil showing epithelioid granulomas and areas of caseous necrosis. Coloration of Ziehl-Neelsen is frequently positive in this location, showing acid-fast bacilli.10 Syphilis has diverse presentations and is referred to as the “great masquerader.” Given this and the increasing incidence of syphilis, a nontreponemal blood test could be included in the diagnosis approach when facing persistent sore throat and lymphadenopathy.

case_info.explanation: Almost 1 year after initial presentation, a pathology review of the tonsils found strong positive immunostaining of antitreponemal antibody (Figure 2) associated with a rapid plasma reagin (RPR) blood titer of 1:4. Treponemal antibody test (chemiluminescent immunoassay) confirmed the syphilis diagnosis. The patient received intramuscular injections of 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin G once a week for 3 weeks, with rapid and complete regression of his symptoms. Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection with increased incidence in high-income countries over the past several decades,1with the majority of cases found in men who have sex with men. Acquired syphilis is divided into early syphilis (primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis [ie, acquired within 1 year]) and late syphilis (late latent and tertiary syphilis [ie, acquired after 1 or more years or unknown duration]). Primary syphilis typically begins with a painless ulcer at the site of infection, which can be overlooked when located in the oropharynx, vagina, or rectum. Consequently, many individuals consult clinicians during the secondary stage, which can have various presentations, the most common being a generalized, nonitchy, erythematous maculopapular rash affecting the palms of the hands and soles of the feet. Herein, retrospective analysis of the cutaneous eruption 1 year before otolaryngologist referral could suggest secondary syphilis, although RPR and treponemal antibody tests were not performed at that time. Secondary syphilis comprises other symptoms, such as lymphadenopathy, fever, and asthenia. After untreated infection, tertiary syphilis can develop, leading to severe neurological and cardiac complications. Syphilis of the tonsils rarely presents as a symptom of secondary syphilis. At this stage, the condition presents as bilateral tonsillitis rather than unilateral tonsillitis, as in primary syphilis.2Although tonsils usually exhibit redness, swelling, and a gray exudate, often with a diffuse pharyngitis, initial clinical examination can be normal, and tonsillitis is only revealed by positron emission tomography/CT.3,4It is predominantly associated with cervical or generalized lymphadenopathy. Diagnosis is often delayed and performed using a histopathological analysis (tonsil or lymph node) and fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption. Confirmation with treponemal antibody test is required because of high false positivity rate of RPR, up to 15%, and treponemal immunohistochemical stain is not specific ofTreponema pallidumand can cross-react with commensal spirochetes of the gastrointestinal tract. Because syphilis cases are increased among men who have sex with men, thorough sexual history might also orientate laboratory workup.5 Regarding differential diagnoses, Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease is a benign evolving necrotizing histiocytic lymphadenitis mainly described in Asia. It occurs in young women in the context of an infectious or autoimmune condition. It typically presents with painful persistent cervical lymphadenopathy associated with fever and leukopenia.6Excisional biopsy of a lymph node is essential for the diagnosis, showing paracortical areas of fibrinoid necrosis, abundant karyorrhexis, and mononuclear cell infiltration.7 Tonsils are a frequent site of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the Waldeyer ring.8It is a rare subtype of extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma occurring predominantly in older men and presenting as odynophagia with cervical lymphadenopathy. Histopathological analysis shows proliferation of large-sized tumor cells with pleomorphic nuclei and immunohistochemistry stains positive for B-cell antigens with a high Ki67 proliferation index.9 Primary tonsillar tuberculosis represents a rare presentation of extrapulmonary tuberculosis. Patients present with recurrent or chronic tonsillitis associated with cervical lymphadenopathy and coexisting pulmonary disease. Diagnosis is based on histopathological examination of the tonsil showing epithelioid granulomas and areas of caseous necrosis. case_info.explanation: Almost 1 year after initial presentation, a pathology review of the tonsils found strong positive immunostaining of antitreponemal antibody (Figure 2) associated with a rapid plasma reagin (RPR) blood titer of 1:4. Treponemal antibody test (chemiluminescent immunoassay) confirmed the syphilis diagnosis. The patient received intramuscular injections of 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin G once a week for 3 weeks, with rapid and complete regression of his symptoms. Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection with increased incidence in high-income countries over the past several decades,1with the majority of cases found in men who have sex with men. Acquired syphilis is divided into early syphilis (primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis [ie, acquired within 1 year]) and late syphilis (late latent and tertiary syphilis [ie, acquired after 1 or more years or unknown duration]). Primary syphilis typically begins with a painless ulcer at the site of infection, which can be overlooked when located in the oropharynx, vagina, or rectum. Consequently, many individuals consult clinicians during the secondary stage, which can have various presentations, the most common being a generalized, nonitchy, erythematous maculopapular rash affecting the palms of the hands and soles of the feet. Herein, retrospective analysis of the cutaneous eruption 1 year before otolaryngologist referral could suggest secondary syphilis, although RPR and treponemal antibody tests were not performed at that time. Secondary syphilis comprises other symptoms, such as lymphadenopathy, fever, and asthenia. After untreated infection, tertiary syphilis can develop, leading to severe neurological and cardiac complications. Syphilis of the tonsils rarely presents as a symptom of secondary syphilis. At this stage, the condition presents as bilateral tonsillitis rather than unilateral tonsillitis, as in primary syphilis.2Although tonsils usually exhibit redness, swelling, and a gray exudate, often with a diffuse pharyngitis, initial clinical examination can be normal, and tonsillitis is only revealed by positron emission tomography/CT.3,4It is predominantly associated with cervical or generalized lymphadenopathy. Diagnosis is often delayed and performed using a histopathological analysis (tonsil or lymph node) and fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption. Confirmation with treponemal antibody test is required because of high false positivity rate of RPR, up to 15%, and treponemal immunohistochemical stain is not specific ofTreponema pallidumand can cross-react with commensal spirochetes of the gastrointestinal tract. Because syphilis cases are increased among men who have sex with men, thorough sexual history might also orientate laboratory workup.5 Regarding differential diagnoses, Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease is a benign evolving necrotizing histiocytic lymphadenitis mainly described in Asia. It occurs in young women in the context of an infectious or autoimmune condition. It typically presents with painful persistent cervical lymphadenopathy associated with fever and leukopenia.6Excisional biopsy of a lymph node is essential for the diagnosis, showing paracortical areas of fibrinoid necrosis, abundant karyorrhexis, and mononuclear cell infiltration.7 Tonsils are a frequent site of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the Waldeyer ring.8It is a rare subtype of extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma occurring predominantly in older men and presenting as odynophagia with cervical lymphadenopathy. Histopathological analysis shows proliferation of large-sized tumor cells with pleomorphic nuclei and immunohistochemistry stains positive for B-cell antigens with a high Ki67 proliferation index.9 Primary tonsillar tuberculosis represents a rare presentation of extrapulmonary tuberculosis. Patients present with recurrent or chronic tonsillitis associated with cervical lymphadenopathy and coexisting pulmonary disease. Diagnosis is based on histopathological examination of the tonsil showing epithelioid granulomas and areas of caseous necrosis. Coloration of Ziehl-Neelsen is frequently positive in this location, showing acid-fast bacilli.10 Syphilis has diverse presentations and is referred to as the “great masquerader.” Given this and the increasing incidence of syphilis, a nontreponemal blood test could be included in the diagnosis approach when facing persistent sore throat and lymphadenopathy.

case_info.explanation: Almost 1 year after initial presentation, a pathology review of the tonsils found strong positive immunostaining of antitreponemal antibody (Figure 2) associated with a rapid plasma reagin (RPR) blood titer of 1:4. Treponemal antibody test (chemiluminescent immunoassay) confirmed the syphilis diagnosis. The patient received intramuscular injections of 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin G once a week for 3 weeks, with rapid and complete regression of his symptoms. Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection with increased incidence in high-income countries over the past several decades,1with the majority of cases found in men who have sex with men. Acquired syphilis is divided into early syphilis (primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis [ie, acquired within 1 year]) and late syphilis (late latent and tertiary syphilis [ie, acquired after 1 or more years or unknown duration]). Primary syphilis typically begins with a painless ulcer at the site of infection, which can be overlooked when located in the oropharynx, vagina, or rectum. Consequently, many individuals consult clinicians during the secondary stage, which can have various presentations, the most common being a generalized, nonitchy, erythematous maculopapular rash affecting the palms of the hands and soles of the feet. Herein, retrospective analysis of the cutaneous eruption 1 year before otolaryngologist referral could suggest secondary syphilis, although RPR and treponemal antibody tests were not performed at that time. Secondary syphilis comprises other symptoms, such as lymphadenopathy, fever, and asthenia. After untreated infection, tertiary syphilis can develop, leading to severe neurological and cardiac complications. Syphilis of the tonsils rarely presents as a symptom of secondary syphilis. Diagnosis is often delayed and performed using a histopathological analysis (tonsil or lymph node) and fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption. Confirmation with treponemal antibody test is required because of high false positivity rate of RPR, up to 15%, and treponemal immunohistochemical stain is not specific ofTreponema pallidumand can cross-react with commensal spirochetes of the gastrointestinal tract. Because syphilis cases are increased among men who have sex with men, thorough sexual history might also orientate laboratory workup.5 Regarding differential diagnoses, Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease is a benign evolving necrotizing histiocytic lymphadenitis mainly described in Asia. It occurs in young women in the context of an infectious or autoimmune condition. It typically presents with painful persistent cervical lymphadenopathy associated with fever and leukopenia.6Excisional biopsy of a lymph node is essential for the diagnosis, showing paracortical areas of fibrinoid necrosis, abundant karyorrhexis, and mononuclear cell infiltration.7 Tonsils are a frequent site of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the Waldeyer ring.8It is a rare subtype of extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma occurring predominantly in older men and presenting as odynophagia with cervical lymphadenopathy. Histopathological analysis shows proliferation of large-sized tumor cells with pleomorphic nuclei and immunohistochemistry stains positive for B-cell antigens with a high Ki67 proliferation index.9 Primary tonsillar tuberculosis represents a rare presentation of extrapulmonary tuberculosis. Patients present with recurrent or chronic tonsillitis associated with cervical lymphadenopathy and coexisting pulmonary disease. Diagnosis is based on histopathological examination of the tonsil showing epithelioid granulomas and areas of caseous necrosis. Coloration of Ziehl-Neelsen is frequently positive in this location, showing acid-fast bacilli.10 Syphilis has diverse presentations and is referred to as the “great masquerader.” Given this and the increasing incidence of syphilis, a nontreponemal blood test could be included in the diagnosis approach when facing persistent sore throat and lymphadenopathy.

case_info.explanation: Almost 1 year after initial presentation, a pathology review of the tonsils found strong positive immunostaining of antitreponemal antibody (Figure 2) associated with a rapid plasma reagin (RPR) blood titer of 1:4. Treponemal antibody test (chemiluminescent immunoassay) confirmed the syphilis diagnosis. The patient received intramuscular injections of 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin G once a week for 3 weeks, with rapid and complete regression of his symptoms. Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection with increased incidence in high-income countries over the past several decades,1with the majority of cases found in men who have sex with men. Acquired syphilis is divided into early syphilis (primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis [ie, acquired within 1 year]) and late syphilis (late latent and tertiary syphilis [ie, acquired after 1 or more years or unknown duration]). Primary syphilis typically begins with a painless ulcer at the site of infection, which can be overlooked when located in the oropharynx, vagina, or rectum. Consequently, many individuals consult clinicians during the secondary stage, which can have various presentations, the most common being a generalized, nonitchy, erythematous maculopapular rash affecting the palms of the hands and soles of the feet. Herein, retrospective analysis of the cutaneous eruption 1 year before otolaryngologist referral could suggest secondary syphilis, although RPR and treponemal antibody tests were not performed at that time. Secondary syphilis comprises other symptoms, such as lymphadenopathy, fever, and asthenia. After untreated infection, tertiary syphilis can develop, leading to severe neurological and cardiac complications. Syphilis of the tonsils rarely presents as a symptom of secondary syphilis. At this stage, the condition presents as bilateral tonsillitis rather than unilateral tonsillitis, as in primary syphilis.2Although tonsils usually exhibit redness, swelling, and a gray exudate, often with a diffuse pharyngitis, initial clinical examination can be normal, and tonsillitis is only revealed by positron emission tomography/CT.3,4It is predominantly associated with cervical or generalized lymphadenopathy. Diagnosis is often delayed and performed using a histopathological analysis (tonsil or lymph node) and fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption. Confirmation with treponemal antibody test is required because of high false positivity rate of RPR, up to 15%, and treponemal immunohistochemical stain is not specific ofTreponema pallidumand can cross-react with commensal spirochetes of the gastrointestinal tract. Because syphilis cases are increased among men who have sex with men, thorough sexual history might also orientate laboratory workup.5 Regarding differential diagnoses, Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease is a benign evolving necrotizing histiocytic lymphadenitis mainly described in Asia. It occurs in young women in the context of an infectious or autoimmune condition. It typically presents with painful persistent cervical lymphadenopathy associated with fever and leukopenia.6Excisional biopsy of a lymph node is essential for the diagnosis, showing paracortical areas of fibrinoid necrosis, abundant karyorrhexis, and mononuclear cell infiltration.7 Tonsils are a frequent site of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the Waldeyer ring.8It is a rare subtype of extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma occurring predominantly in older men and presenting as odynophagia with cervical lymphadenopathy. Histopathological analysis shows proliferation of large-sized tumor cells with pleomorphic nuclei and immunohistochemistry stains positive for B-cell antigens with a high Ki67 proliferation index.9 Primary tonsillar tuberculosis represents a rare presentation of extrapulmonary tuberculosis. Patients present with recurrent or chronic tonsillitis associated with cervical lymphadenopathy and coexisting pulmonary disease. Diagnosis is based on histopathological examination of the tonsil showing epithelioid granulomas and areas of caseous necrosis. Coloration of Ziehl-Neelsen is frequently positive in this location, showing acid-fast bacilli.10 Syphilis has diverse presentations and is referred to as the “great masquerader.” Given this and the increasing incidence of syphilis, a nontreponemal blood test could be included in the diagnosis approach when facing persistent sore throat and lymphadenopathy.

The patient underwent unilateral tonsillectomy followed by a course of antibiotics and prednisone. On pathologic examination, the tonsils showed lymphoid follicular hyperplasia associated with a polymorphic inflammatory infiltrate without abnormal lymphoid cells and plasmocytes (Figure 1B). Further exploration of the patient’s history revealed that 1 year before the otolaryngology evaluation, he developed a cutaneous eruption on the trunk.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid

   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.caption: A, Transaxial positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) image showing intense bilateral symmetric tonsillar hypermetabolism and bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy hypermetabolism. case_info.explanation: Almost 1 year after initial presentation, a pathology review of the tonsils found strong positive immunostaining of antitreponemal antibody (Figure 2) associated with a rapid plasma reagin (RPR) blood titer of 1:4. Treponemal antibody test (chemiluminescent immunoassay) confirmed the syphilis diagnosis. The patient received intramuscular injections of 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin G once a week for 3 weeks, with rapid and complete regression of his symptoms. Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection with increased incidence in high-income countries over the past several decades,1with the majority of cases found in men who have sex with men. Acquired syphilis is divided into early syphilis (primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis [ie, acquired within 1 year]) and late syphilis (late latent and tertiary syphilis [ie, acquired after 1 or more years or unknown duration]). Primary syphilis typically begins with a painless ulcer at the site of infection, which can be overlooked when located in the oropharynx, vagina, or rectum. Consequently, many individuals consult clinicians during the secondary stage, which can have various presentations, the most common being a generalized, nonitchy, erythematous maculopapular rash affecting the palms of the hands and soles of the feet. Herein, retrospective analysis of the cutaneous eruption 1 year before otolaryngologist referral could suggest secondary syphilis, although RPR and treponemal antibody tests were not performed at that time. Secondary syphilis comprises other symptoms, such as lymphadenopathy, fever, and asthenia. After untreated infection, tertiary syphilis can develop, leading to severe neurological and cardiac complications. Syphilis of the tonsils rarely presents as a symptom of secondary syphilis. At this stage, the condition presents as bilateral tonsillitis rather than unilateral tonsillitis, as in primary syphilis.2Although tonsils usually exhibit redness, swelling, and a gray exudate, often with a diffuse pharyngitis, initial clinical examination can be normal, and tonsillitis is only revealed by positron emission tomography/CT.3,4It is predominantly associated with cervical or generalized lymphadenopathy. Diagnosis is often delayed and performed using a histopathological analysis (tonsil or lymph node) and fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption. Confirmation with treponemal antibody test is required because of high false positivity rate of RPR, up to 15%, and treponemal immunohistochemical stain is not specific ofTreponema pallidumand can cross-react with commensal spirochetes of the gastrointestinal tract. Because syphilis cases are increased among men who have sex with men, thorough sexual history might also orientate laboratory workup.5 Regarding differential diagnoses, Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease is a benign evolving necrotizing histiocytic lymphadenitis mainly described in Asia. It occurs in young women in the context of an infectious or autoimmune condition. It typically presents with painful persistent cervical lymphadenopathy associated with fever and leukopenia.6Excisional biopsy of a lymph node is essential for the diagnosis, showing paracortical areas of fibrinoid necrosis, abundant karyorrhexis, and mononuclear cell infiltration.7 Tonsils are a frequent site of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the Waldeyer ring.8It is a rare subtype of extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma occurring predominantly in older men and presenting as odynophagia with cervical lymphadenopathy. Histopathological analysis shows proliferation of large-sized tumor cells with pleomorphic nuclei and immunohistochemistry stains positive for B-cell antigens with a high Ki67 proliferation index.9 Primary tonsillar tuberculosis represents a rare presentation of extrapulmonary tuberculosis. Patients present with recurrent or chronic tonsillitis associated with cervical lymphadenopathy and coexisting pulmonary disease. Diagnosis is based on histopathological examination of the tonsil showing epithelioid granulomas and areas of caseous necrosis. Coloration of Ziehl-Neelsen is frequently positive in this location, showing acid-fast bacilli.10 Syphilis has diverse presentations and is referred to as the “great masquerader.” Given this and the increasing incidence of syphilis, a nontreponemal blood test could be included in the diagnosis approach when facing persistent sore throat and lymphadenopathy.
